planting.note: Direct sow in autumn to catch the first seasonal rains, mimicking natural germination timing on rocky Mediterranean hillsides; established clumps resprout from a deep taproot each year.

directions: Sow seed in fall into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil and let plants establish a deep taproot over their first year; harvest in early-to-mid spring, before the flower stalk fully opens, by cutting the thorny young stems and unopened flower-head clusters while still tender. Akkoub is a cornerstone foraged spring vegetable across the hill country of Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria, where the peeled stems and artichoke-like hearts are simmered into stews, fried with eggs, or cooked with yogurt and lamb; the flavor and texture are often compared to globe artichoke. Wear gloves when handling and trim away the spiny bracts before cooking. Because wild populations have been heavily pressure-harvested in parts of its native range, growing it from seed in a home garden plot is a useful way to take pressure off foraged stands.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online: Gundelia tournefortii
Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine — wild edible plants of the Levant

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted stock in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Nabali is one of the oldest and most widely planted olive cultivars in the central hill country of the West Bank.

directions: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and expect modest irrigation needs once the deep root system is established; Nabali is a dual-purpose Palestinian heirloom olive grown for centuries for both high-quality oil and brine-cured green table olives. It flowers and fruits reliably but benefits from a second nearby cultivar to improve pollination and fruit set. Pick green-to-straw-colored fruit in early fall for curing, or allow it to darken further into winter for a richer, higher-yield oil press. Prune lightly each year after harvest to maintain an open canopy and encourage new fruiting wood.
sources: International Olive Council — World Catalogue of Olive Varieties

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted stock in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Souri is the principal oil-pressing olive of Lebanon and coastal Syria.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil along warm coastal or lowland sites; Souri is the dominant oil-pressing olive cultivar of Lebanon and coastal Syria, valued for consistently heavy yields and a smooth, mild-flavored oil. Trees are vigorous and productive but alternate bear to some degree, producing a heavier crop every other year unless thinned and pruned to even out production. Harvest fruit as it turns from green to purple-black in late fall for peak oil content, and press within a day or two of picking for the best flavor. Give young trees supplemental water through their first two to three summers; mature trees are quite drought-tolerant.
sources: International Olive Council — World Catalogue of Olive Varieties

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed; this pale, round-to-cylindrical squash is grown throughout the Levant specifically for stuffing.

directions: Direct sow once soil has warmed, in hills spaced to give the sprawling plants room; harvest fruit young and small, around three to four inches long, when the thin pale-green skin is still tender and the seed cavity is small. Kousa is the light-colored, mild-flavored Levantine squash used for kousa mahshi, hollowed out with a corer and stuffed with rice and spiced ground lamb before braising in tomato sauce or yogurt. Pick every one to two days during peak season, since fruit left on the vine quickly swells, toughens, and develops larger seeds that make hollowing and stuffing harder. Keep plants evenly watered and pick off any overripe fruit promptly to keep the vine producing.

common_name: Ful Medames Fava Bean (Small-Seeded Egyptian Brown Fava)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.

directions: Sow seed early, spacing plants more closely than large-seeded fava types since this is a compact, small-seeded selection bred for dense pod set rather than individual bean size. Ful Medames is the small, brown-skinned fava named for the classic Egyptian breakfast dish of the same name, in which the whole beans — skins left on — are simmered for hours until completely soft, then mashed with garlic, lemon, cumin, and olive oil. The smaller seed size shortens the long stovetop cooking time somewhat compared with large fava varieties, though the dish is still traditionally cooked low and slow. Pinch growing tips after the first flush of pods sets to curb aphids and push more energy into pod fill, and harvest once pods have dried on the plant if saving beans for the signature stewed preparation.
sources: Agricultural Research Center (ARC), Egypt — Field Crops Research Institute

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Shamouti originated in 19th-century Ottoman Palestine near the port of Jaffa, giving rise to its international name, the Jaffa orange.

directions: Plant grafted trees in full sun in well-drained soil and water regularly through the first several seasons while the root system establishes. Shamouti, known worldwide as the Jaffa orange, became famous in the 19th and early 20th centuries as one of the first citrus cultivars sturdy enough for long sea voyages, thanks to its thick, easy-peeling rind and nearly seedless, low-acid flesh. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree without overripening quickly, making harvest timing fairly forgiving. The tree is self-compatible and fruits reliably on its own, with lightly fragrant, sparse blossoms compared to some other sweet orange cultivars.
sources: University of California, Riverside — Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Helda Pole Bean (Lebanese Flat Romano Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed at the base of a sturdy 6 to 8 foot trellis or pole; this vigorous climbing Romano-type bean is a staple in Lebanese market gardens.

directions: Direct sow at the base of a tall, sturdy support once soil has warmed, since vines will climb vigorously to six feet or more and need the structure to stay productive and easy to pick. Helda produces broad, flat, pale-green pods eight to ten inches long that stay tender and nearly stringless even at a larger size, making it well suited to loubieh bi zeit, the braised green bean and olive oil dish common across Lebanese and wider eastern Mediterranean tables. Pick every two to three days once pods begin forming to keep plants setting new flowers rather than diverting energy into maturing seed. Provide consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill for the best yield and texture.
